item.title: Spring Boot on Kubernetes: memory, probes and shutting down politely
item.description: Our Spring Boot services run on Kubernetes now. Getting a jar into a container and a container into a cluster is the easy part, and there are a hundred tutorials for it. These are the things that are easy to get wrong after that, and that every Java service on Kubernetes needs to get right. 1. The JVM and the container memory limit You give the pod a memory limit, say 1 GiB.

item.title: RabbitMQ with Spring Boot: retries, dead letters and the message that comes twice
item.description: When a seafarer finishes an assessment, several things have to happen: the result is scored and stored, reports are updated, the LMS that launched the test gets the outcome, maybe a certificate is generated. None of that should make the person wait, and none of it should fail because one of those systems is having a bad day. So “attempt finished” is an event on RabbitMQ, and each of those things is a consumer.

item.title: One door for every client: an API gateway as a facade
item.description: As we split the old platform into Spring Boot services, we got a new problem very quickly: there are now many services, and many kinds of clients. The web app, the assessment UI, LMS integrations, the clients used on board ships. If every client talks to every service directly, every client has to know where every service lives, how it authenticates, and how its API looks this month. So all clients go through one entry point: an API gateway that acts as a facade over the services behind it.

item.title: Elasticsearch as a primary database: what I wish someone had told me
item.description: Two years ago I used Elasticsearch as a read model: MySQL was the truth, Elasticsearch was a copy built for searching, and if the copy broke you rebuilt it. On the platform I work on now, Elasticsearch is the truth. Users, content, results: the primary store for a lot of the data is an Elasticsearch cluster. It wasn’t my decision, and I’m not going to argue it was right or wrong.

item.title: Never lose an answer: offline-first answer saving for exams at sea
item.description: Back in May I wrote about what satellite internet on a ship means for an online exam. The rule I cared about most was: never lose an answer. The connection can go away at any point, for minutes, and the person taking the test should be able to keep going. This is how we’re approaching it. Not finished, but the shape is clear. Step 1: load the whole test up front When the attempt starts, the client fetches everything it needs in one go: all items, the media they use, the navigation rules.

item.title: The exam state that lived in a singleton
Running QTI 2.1 assessments in Java with JQTI+
item.description: For the new assessment platform we decided not to invent our own format for questions and tests. There is a standard for this, IMS QTI (Question and Test Interoperability), and version 2.1 is what most tools speak. Using it means authors can bring content from other tools, and our tests are not locked into our own database schema. The last few weeks I built a proof of concept: load a QTI test, step through it, submit answers, get a score.

item.title: Exams over satellite internet: designing for the worst network you can imagine
item.description: New year, new job. I’m now at Videotel, working on the platform that the maritime industry uses for training and assessment of seafarers. Crew members take tests when they apply for a job, and they take training and assessments on board, while the ship is at sea. The second part is what makes this interesting. Most of what I knew about web apps assumes the network is fast and basically always there.

item.title: What I learned as the first in-house engineer
item.description: At the end of this month I’m leaving HolaLuz. I joined when the company was small and its software was built by an external agency. I was the first engineer hired to own it in-house. When I leave, there’s a team of developers, a CI pipeline, infrastructure as code, and a system that fails in smaller and more boring ways than it used to. This is not a goodbye post, it’s notes for myself on what I would tell someone starting in the same position.

item.title: Immutable servers with Packer, Ansible and Terraform
item.description: Over the past months I spent a lot of my time on the operations side at work. The main change was going from servers that we configure in place to servers that we never change after they start. If something needs to change, we build a new image and replace the server. Here’s how the pieces fit, because the hardest part for me was not learning each tool but understanding where one stops and the next one starts.

item.title: Our first step out of the monolith was a read model
item.description: When people talk about breaking up a monolith, the first picture is usually “take the payments code, put it in its own service with its own database”. We haven’t done that yet. What we did first was less dramatic and, I think, the right first step: we took one read path out of the main database. The problem Our back-office tool lets people search customers and contracts by name, address, ID document, supply point code, partial phone number and a few other things, in any combination.

item.title: From a day to an hour: fanning out invoice work over SQS
item.description: Every billing cycle we have to process invoices for all of our customers: pull them from the ERP, store them, make them visible in the customer area, and keep the related contracts in sync. For a long time this was one big job that went through the invoices one by one. It took about a day. The worst part was not the duration, it was what happened when it failed at 70%: figure out where it stopped, fix the data, start again, hope.

item.title: Keeping an OAuth2 integration alive with the Laravel scheduler
item.description: Our lead pipeline at work pushes every new sign-up into a marketing CRM (Infusionsoft) so the sales and marketing teams can follow up. It talks to the CRM’s REST API using OAuth2. That worked fine for weeks and then, one Monday morning, it didn’t: no new leads in the CRM since Saturday, and every API call failed with an invalid token error. Somebody had to log in to the CRM in a browser and authorize our app again.

item.title: Upgrading to Laravel 5.3: where did lists() go?
item.description: As promised in the last post, here are some notes from the Laravel 5.3 upgrade we did on the customer portal at work. The codebase is almost two years old, has grown three separate “apps” (customer area, back-office, partner tools) on subdomains, and was started on Laravel 5.0. So not a huge app, but big enough that “just run the tests” is not the whole story. Most of the upgrade guide went smoothly.

item.title: Card payments with Redsys: trust the notification, not the redirect
item.description: Over the last couple of months at HolaLuz I worked on letting customers pay overdue electricity invoices by card, directly from the customer area and from our internal back-office tool. In Spain this almost always means Redsys, the payment gateway behind most bank “TPV virtual” contracts. The integration itself is not complicated, and there are decent PHP libraries for it. But a few things only became clear once real money started moving, so I’m writing them down while I still remember.
